title: Kenya Park Fees: KWS, Masai Mara and Conservancy Rates Explained
meta_title: Kenya Park Fees: 15 Parks' Rates and 6 Smart Savings
meta_description: Kenya park fees for Amboseli, Tsavo, Nakuru, Nairobi and the Masai Mara, plus package savings and cashless payment. Plan your safari budget with confidence.
excerpt: Kenya park fees explained: current KWS rates for every major park, the seasonal Masai Mara fee, conservancy charges, package savings and how to pay.
content:
Kenya park fees for foreign visitors run from US$25 to US$90 per adult per 24 hours in Kenya Wildlife Service parks, while the Masai Mara National Reserve charges US$100 a day from January to June and US$200 from July to December (checked October 2026). Children pay roughly half, and conservancies set their own rates.

Kenya park fees are the one safari cost you cannot negotiate, and they are charged per person, per park, per day, so they add up quickly on a multi-park trip. This guide lists every major rate in one place, explains the package tickets that save money, shows how payment works now that KWS has moved to a cashless system, and adds the fees up for a sample week.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Quick Facts

  • Amboseli and Lake Nakuru: US$90 per non-resident adult, US$45 per child, per 24 hours (checked October 2026)
  • Nairobi, Tsavo East and Tsavo West: US$80 per adult, US$40 per child (checked October 2026)
  • Masai Mara reserve: US$100 per adult per day January-June, US$200 July-December (checked October 2026)
  • Free entry: Children aged five and under in KWS parks
  • How to pay: Cashless only: M-Pesa, card, bank transfer or eWallet through KWSPay on eCitizen
  • Current KWS rates: In force since 1 October 2025; confirm before you book

What Are Kenya Park Fees and Who Sets Them?

Kenya park fees are daily conservation charges paid to whoever manages the protected area you enter. Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) sets one national schedule for national parks such as Amboseli, Tsavo and Lake Nakuru, county governments set fees for national reserves such as the Masai Mara and Samburu, and private conservancies set their own.

This split matters when you plan. A KWS park fee is the same whichever operator you travel with, and it changes only when new regulations are gazetted, as happened on 1 October 2025. County reserve fees can change with a county finance act, and conservancy fees are often bundled into the nightly rate of the camp you stay in, so you may never see them as a separate line.

The Kenya park fees you pay also depend on who you are. KWS uses four groups: East African citizens and Kenya residents pay in Kenya shillings, while non-residents and citizens of other African countries pay in US dollars. A Kenya resident is a non-Kenyan living in Kenya on a valid resident permit, so bring the permit if you want that rate.

Kenya Park Fees for KWS National Parks

Kenya park fees in KWS parks fall into price bands. Amboseli and Lake Nakuru are the premium parks at US$90 per non-resident adult, Nairobi and both Tsavo parks cost US$80, Meru, Aberdare and Kora cost US$70, and scenic parks such as Hell's Gate cost US$50 (checked October 2026).

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Park or bandNon-resident adultNon-resident childKenya resident adult

Tsavo East, Tsavo WestUS$80US$40KES 1,350

Marine parks (Watamu, Malindi, Kisite Mpunguti, Mombasa, Diani-Chale)US$25US$15KES 675

All figures come from the Kenya Wildlife Service conservation fee schedule and were checked in October 2026. Each ticket covers a single entry for up to 24 hours, so leaving the park and coming back the same day means paying again. Children are aged 5 to under 18, students up to 23 on an organised school trip pay the child rate, and children aged five and under are free.

Kenya park fees for East African and African citizens

East African citizens, which includes Kenyans, pay KES 1,500 for Amboseli and Lake Nakuru and KES 1,000 for Nairobi and Tsavo. Citizens of other African countries pay a separate dollar rate: US$50 for the premium parks and US$40 for Nairobi and Tsavo. KWS also exempts Kenyan citizens aged 70 and over, persons with disabilities, and registered drivers and guides.

Which Kenya national park is the cheapest to visit?

Among the classic safari parks, Meru and Aberdare are the cheapest at US$70, and Meru has big-game country with far fewer vehicles than Amboseli. If you only want a short wildlife fix, scenic parks such as Hell's Gate at US$50 or the Nairobi Animal Orphanage at US$25 are the lowest-cost options.

Can You Save Money With KWS Package Tickets?

Yes. KWS sells combined tickets that cost less than paying for each park separately. The Tsavo West and Amboseli package costs US$150 per non-resident adult instead of US$170, and the Tsavo East, Tsavo West and Amboseli package costs US$215 instead of US$250 (checked October 2026).

Photo: Divulge Adventures

PackageNon-resident adultSeparate ticketsSaving per adult
Tsavo West and AmboseliUS$150US$170US$20
Tsavo East, Tsavo West and AmboseliUS$215US$250US$35
Nairobi package (park, Animal Orphanage, Safari Walk)US$105US$130US$25
Nairobi Animal Orphanage and Safari WalkUS$40US$50US$10

Packages cut Kenya park fees most on the classic southern circuit from Nairobi to Amboseli and on through Tsavo West to the coast, a route many travellers combine with a beach stay. Ask your operator whether the package covers your exact dates, because the ticket is built around consecutive park visits rather than one stay in each park weeks apart.

How Much Is the Masai Mara Entrance Fee?

The Masai Mara National Reserve is run by Narok County, not KWS, and its fee is seasonal. Non-resident adults paid US$100 per day from January to June and US$200 per day from July to December, with children aged 9 to 17 at US$50 and children aged 8 and under free (checked October 2026).

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Kenyan citizens paid KES 1,500 in the first half of the year and KES 3,000 in the second, with East African residents at KES 2,500 and KES 5,000. The doubling from July lines up with the Great Migration season, which makes the Mara the single biggest item in Kenya park fees on most safaris. Our full guide to the Masai Mara entrance fee covers gates, the Mara Triangle and rules for day visitors in more depth.

The cheapest way to lower Kenya park fees in the Mara is timing. Visiting in January to March, or in the green season of April to June, halves the daily reserve charge, and many camps also cut their own rates in those months. If you want the river crossings, budget for the higher fee and spend fewer, better-placed nights rather than more nights in the wrong area.

What Do Kenya Conservancies and Private Reserves Charge?

Conservancies sit outside the national Kenya park fees schedule and set their own, usually higher, rates because they fund land leases paid to local landowners. Ol Pejeta Conservancy, for example, charges US$110 per non-resident adult and US$55 per child aged 3 to 11 per day, according to its 2026 tariff (checked October 2026).

Photo: Divulge Adventures

The Ol Pejeta Conservancy tariff guide also lists a separate East African citizen rate of KES 2,000 per adult. Our Ol Pejeta Conservancy guide explains what that fee gives you access to, including the chimpanzee sanctuary and the last northern white rhinos.

In the conservancies that border the Masai Mara, such as Mara North, Olare Motorogi and Naboisho, the conservancy fee is normally built into your camp rate and is not sold at a gate. That is why a conservancy camp can look expensive next to a reserve lodge; the comparison only works once you add the reserve fee to the reserve lodge price. Samburu, Buffalo Springs and Shaba are county-run reserves with their own rates, which we confirm at the time of booking.

Other Kenya Park Fees: Vehicles, Camping and Activities

On top of the entry fee, Kenya park fees include charges for the vehicle and for special activities. A safari vehicle with fewer than six seats pays KES 600 a day and one with 6-12 seats KES 1,500, while activities such as night game drives and walking safaris are priced per person (checked October 2026).

Parking fees also apply at a few busy sites, including Hell's Gate and Lake Nakuru, but visitors holding a paid entry ticket are exempt. If an after-dark drive is on your wish list, our guide to night game drives in Kenya explains where they are allowed and what you see. In the Masai Mara, reserve ranger escorts and vehicle fees are set separately by the county.

How Do You Pay Kenya Park Fees?

Kenya park fees are paid cashless. Since 1 November 2025 KWS has used KWSPay, an upgraded eCitizen platform, which accepts M-Pesa, bank cards, bank transfers and eWallets. Cash is not part of the system, so do not arrive at a KWS gate expecting to pay in dollar notes.

On a guided safari your operator pays all Kenya park fees in advance and includes it in your quote, so all you need at the gate is your passport, or your resident permit or national ID if you are claiming a local rate. Independent travellers should pay online before arriving. Card payments can carry a charge of up to 3.5% depending on the card provider, and KWS converts using a monthly exchange rate.

In the Masai Mara, the main county gates take US dollars and Kenya shillings, but the Mara Triangle side is cashless and takes Visa, Mastercard and M-Pesa. Remember that Kenya park fees are separate from entry to Kenya itself: most visitors also need a Kenya eTA before flying.

How Much Do Kenya Park Fees Add Up to on a 7-Day Safari?

On a typical 7-day Amboseli, Lake Nakuru and Masai Mara safari in the July-December high season, park fees come to roughly US$870 per non-resident adult, or about US$570 if the same trip runs between January and June. This is an estimate per person and excludes vehicle fees and conservancy fees.

Park and daysHigh season (Jul-Dec)Low season (Jan-Jun)
Amboseli, 2 daysUS$180US$180
Lake Nakuru, 1 dayUS$90US$90
Masai Mara reserve, 3 daysUS$600US$300
Estimated total per adultAbout US$870About US$570

The number of fee days depends on how your nights and drive days fall, because each KWS ticket lasts 24 hours and the Mara is charged per day. Kenya park fees are only one part of the budget, so see our complete Kenya safari cost breakdown for lodges, transport and tips. Lake Naivasha, a common stop on this route, has no national park fee for the lake itself.

Insider Tips

  • Time the Mara: January to June halves the Masai Mara reserve fee
  • Use packages: Tsavo and Amboseli combined tickets save US$20-35 per adult
  • Mind the 24 hours: Leaving a KWS park and re-entering means a new ticket
  • Carry documents: Bring your passport, resident permit or ID to the gate
  • Check inclusions: Ask whether park and conservancy fees are in your quote
  • Budget for change: Fees rise with new regulations, so confirm before paying

Frequently Asked Questions

How much are Kenya park fees for tourists?

Kenya park fees for foreign tourists range from US$25 for marine parks to US$90 per adult per 24 hours for Amboseli and Lake Nakuru (checked October 2026). The Masai Mara reserve charges US$100 a day from January to June and US$200 from July to December. Children pay about half.

Can I pay Kenya park fees in cash?

No, KWS park fees cannot be paid in cash. Since November 2025 Kenya Wildlife Service has used the cashless KWSPay system on eCitizen, which takes M-Pesa, bank cards, bank transfers and eWallets. The main Masai Mara county gates still take US dollars and Kenya shillings, but the Mara Triangle is cashless. On a guided safari your operator pays all fees in advance.

Are park fees included in a Kenya safari price?

Park fees are included in most guided Kenya safari prices, but you should always check. A good quote lists the parks, the number of fee days and whether conservancy fees are covered. Divulge Adventures shows park fees in every tailor-made quote, so you know exactly what you are paying for before you book and nothing is collected from you at the gate.

Do children pay Kenya park fees?

Children aged 5 to under 18 pay a child rate in KWS parks, usually half the adult fee, such as US$45 for Amboseli, and children aged five and under enter free (checked October 2026). In the Masai Mara National Reserve, non-resident children aged 9 to 17 paid US$50 per day and children aged 8 and under were free. Conservancies use their own age bands.

Is the Masai Mara fee paid to KWS?

No, the Masai Mara National Reserve fee is not paid to KWS. The reserve is managed by Narok County, with the Mara Triangle section run by a separate management body, so its fees follow a different schedule from Kenya Wildlife Service parks. That is why the Mara fee is seasonal, at US$100 per day from January to June and US$200 from July to December.

Final Thoughts

Kenya park fees run from US$25 to US$90 a day in KWS parks, with the Masai Mara the big variable at US$100 or US$200 depending on the month. Plan your route around package tickets, the Mara season and fewer, longer stays, and the fees become a predictable part of the budget.

Kenya park fees change, so treat these figures as a planning guide and confirm before paying. If you would rather not do the sums, send us your dates and we will build a safari with all Kenya park fees counted in.
